or
$r=\frac{n}{2 \pi} \cdot\left(\frac{h}{m v}\right) \text { or } r=\frac{n \lambda}{2 \pi}$
(From de -Broglie equation, $\lambda=\frac{h}{m v}$ )
for fourth orbit $n=4\begin{gathered}

\therefore \text { circumference }=2 \pi r=2 \pi \times \frac{2 \lambda}{\pi}=4 \lambda
\end{gathered}$

$\begin{array}{llrl}
\Rightarrow & \frac{1}{y^4} \frac{d y}{d x} & =\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{d t}{d x} \\

& \Rightarrow & \frac{d t}{d x}+\frac{3}{x} t & =\frac{3}{x^3} \cos x

$\begin{gathered}
P=\frac{3}{x}, Q=\frac{3}{x^3} \cos x \\

\end{aligned}$

If $\mathbf{E}=-102.4 \times 10^3 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \mathrm{NC}^{-1}$ and $\mathbf{B}=8 \times 10^{-2} \hat{\mathbf{j}} \mathrm{Wbm}^{-2}$ the direction of motion of the particles is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
m & =1 \times 10^{-26} \mathrm{~kg}, q=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C} \\
v & =1.28 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$
Electric field, $\mathbf{E}=-102.4 \times 10^3 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{C}$
Magnetic field, $\mathbf{B}=8 \times 10^{-2} \hat{\mathbf{j}} \mathrm{Wbm}^{-2}\begin{aligned}
\frac{|\mathbf{E}|}{|\mathbf{B}|} & =\frac{102.4 \times 10^3}{8 \times 10^{-2}} \\
& =\frac{10.24 \times 10^6}{8} \\
& =1.28 \times 10^6
\end{aligned}$
Hence,
$|\mathbf{v}|=\frac{|\mathbf{E}|}{|\mathbf{B}|}$
So, particle will remain undeflected, hence direction of motion of particle is along the positive $X$-axis.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body projected vertically upwards crosses a point twice in its journey at a height $h$ just after $t_1$ and $t_2$ seconds. Maximum height reached by the body is
questions.solution:
Time taken by the body to reach the point $A$ is $t_1$ (During upward journey).

The body crosess this point again (during downward journey) after $t_2$, i.e., the body takes the time $\left(t_2-t_1\right)$ to come again at point $A$.

So, the time taken by the body to reach at point $B$ (at maximum height).
$t=t_1+\left(\frac{t_2-t_1}{2}\right)$
[ $\because$ Time of ascending $=$ Time of descending]
$t=\frac{t_1+t_2}{2}$
So, maximum height, $H=\frac{1}{2} g t^2=\frac{1}{2} g\left(\frac{t_1+t_2}{2}\right)^2=2 g\left(\frac{t_1+t_2}{4}\right)^2$

The equation of trajectory of a projectile is $y=10 x-\left(\frac{5}{9}\right) x^2$.

If we assume $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$, the range of projectile (in metre) is
questions.solution:
Equation of projectile is
$y=10 x-\left(\frac{5}{9}\right) x^2$
Standard equation is
$y=x \tan \theta-\frac{g}{2 u^2 \cos ^2 \theta} \cdot x^2$
On comparing,
$\tan \theta=10$
and
$\begin{array}{rlrl} 
& \frac{g}{2 u^2 \cos ^2 \theta} & =\frac{9}{9} \\
\Rightarrow & 10 u^2 \cos ^2 \theta & =9 \mathrm{~g} \\
& \ddots & g & =10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 \\
& \therefore & u^2 \cos ^2 \theta & =9
\end{array}
(given)
$\therefore$ Range of projectile $R=\frac{2 u^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta}{g}\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{2 u^2 \tan \theta \cdot \cos ^2 \theta}{g} \\
& =\frac{2\left(u^2 \cos ^2 \theta\right) \cdot \tan \theta}{g} \\
& =\frac{2 \times 9 \times 10}{10}=18 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion (A) Propagation of light through an optical fibre is due to total internal reflection taking place at the core-clad interface.
Reason (R) Refractive index of the material of the core of the optical fibre is greater than that of air.
options: both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Assertion and Reason Analysis
- Assertion (A): The assertion states that light propagation through an optical fiber is due to total internal reflection (TIR) at the core-clad interface. This is true. Light entering the fiber's core strikes the boundary between the core and the cladding at an angle greater than the critical angle, causing the light to reflect back into the core rather than refracting out. This process repeats, allowing light to travel long distances inside the fiber.
- Reason (R): The reason states that the refractive index of the optical fiber's core is greater than that of air. This is also true. The core is a glass or plastic material with a refractive index typically around 1.5, while air has a refractive index of approximately 1.0.
Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are true statements. However, the reason is not a correct explanation for the assertion. For TIR to occur, the light must travel from a denser medium (higher refractive index) to a rarer medium (lower refractive index). The relevant interface is between the core and the cladding, where the core's refractive index is greater than the cladding's. The relationship between the core's refractive index and air's refractive index is not directly responsible for the TIR phenomenon within the fiber itself.
Therefore, the correct option is (2): both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The focal length of an equi-convex lens is greater than the radius of curvature of any of the surfaces. Then the refractive index of the material of the lens is
options: greater than zero but less than 1.5
questions.solution:
Focal length of lens,
$\frac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2}\right)$
For equi-convex lens,
$\begin{aligned}
R_1 & =+R, R_2=-R \\
\frac{1}{f} & =(\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{-R}\right) \\
\frac{1}{f} & =(\mu-1)\left(\frac{2}{R}\right) \\
f & =\frac{R}{2(\mu-1)} \\
f \lt  R, \text { so, } 2(\mu-1) & \lt  1 \\
(\mu-1) & \lt  \frac{1}{2} \\
\text { i.e. } \quad(\mu-1) & \lt  0.5 \\
\mu & \lt  1.5
\end{aligned}$
Focal length of convex lens is positive. So, $\mu$ cannot be negative, hence $\mu$ should be greater than zero but less than 1.5.

questions.q: The ratio of specific heats of a gas is $\gamma$. The change in internal energy of one mole of the gas, when the volume changes from $V$ to $2 V$ at constant pressure $p$ is
questions.solution:
Change in internal energy,
$d U=d Q-d W$
At constant pressure,
$\begin{aligned}
d U & =C_p d T-p d V \\
& =C_p d T-R d T \\
& =\left(C_p-R\right) d T=C_V d T \\
& =\frac{R}{\gamma-1} d T \\
& =\frac{R}{\gamma-1} \times \frac{p V}{R} \\
& =\frac{p V}{\gamma-1}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A vehicle sounding a whistle of frequency $256 \mathrm{~Hz}$ is moving on a straight road, towards a hill with a velocity of $10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. The number of beats per second observed by a person travelling in the vehicle is velocity of sound $=330 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$

$\begin{aligned}
n^{\prime} & =\left(\frac{v+v_s}{v-v_s}\right) \times n \\
& =\left(\frac{330+10}{330-10}\right) \times 256 \\
& =\frac{340}{320} \times 256=272 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Number of beats heard by the observer
$=272-256=16$

questions.q:
A transverse wave propagating on a stretched string of linear density $3 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$ is represented by the equation $y=0.2 \sin (15 x+60 t)$
where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The tension in the string (in newton) is
questions.solution:
Equation of wave, $y=0.2 \sin (1.5 x+60 t)$ Comparing with standard equation,
$\begin{aligned}
& y=A \sin (k x+\omega t) \\
& k=1.5, \omega=60 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Velocity of wave, $v=\frac{\omega}{k}=\frac{60}{1.5}=40 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
Velocity of wave in a stretched string,
$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}$
where $m=$ linear density
$T=\text { tension in the string }$
So,
$\begin{aligned}
T & =v^2 m \\
& =(40)^2 \times 3 \times 10^{-4}=0.48
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The machine gun fires 240 bullets per minute. If the mass of each bullet is $10 \mathrm{~g}$ and the velocity of the bullets is $600 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$, the power (in kW) of the gun is
questions.solution:
Work done by the gun $=$ Total kinetic energy of the bullets
$\begin{aligned}
& =n \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\
& =240 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10^{-3}(600)^2 \\
& =120 \times 10 \times 10^{-3} \times 600 \times 600
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore \text { Power of gun } & =\frac{\text { work done }}{\text { time taken }} \\ & =\frac{120 \times 10 \times 10^{-3} \times 600 \times 600}{1 \mathrm{~min}} \\ & =\frac{120 \times 10 \times 360}{60} \\ & =120 \times 10 \times 6 \mathrm{~W} \\ & =\frac{120 \times 10 \times 6}{1000} \mathrm{~kW}=7.2 \mathrm{~kW}\end{aligned}$
